title: Fudim v. Commissioner
articleTitle: Judicial Precedents and the Evolution of Substantiation: An Analytical Report on Fudim v. Commissioner and the Modern R&D Tax Credit Landscape
subject: Substantially All / Wage Allocation
summary: Fudim v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 1994-235) is a U.S. Tax Court R&D tax credit case under IRC Section 41 addressing taxpayers without contemporaneous time records. Applying the Cohan rule, the court allowed a sole proprietor's self-employment income, his engineer wife's wages, and research supplies, but disallowed his daughter's wages for lack of evidence of her qualified services.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Factual Context and Technological Innovation

In Fudim v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1994-235, 67 T.C.M. (CCH) 3011 (1994), the United States Tax Court addressed fundamental questions regarding the qualification of research activities, the eligibility of self-employment earnings and family member wages, and the evidentiary threshold required to substantiate Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 in the absence of contemporaneous time-tracking records. Decided on May 26, 1994, by Special Trial Judge Joan Seitz Pate (Docket No. 10309-91), the ruling remains a foundational benchmark in United States federal tax jurisprudence governing the application of the judicial estimation doctrine established in Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), to research and development (R&D) tax credit claims.

The petitioner, Dr. Efrem V. Fudim, was an accomplished research scientist born in Ukraine (then part of the Soviet Union) who earned a doctorate degree from the Institute of Control Sciences of the U.S.S.R. Academy of Sciences in Moscow. After emigrating to the United States in 1979 and settling in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, Dr. Fudim worked in the corporate applied research group at Johnson Controls from 1979 until 1985. By December 1984, he had published 38 scientific papers and been granted 39 patents by various countries; he is also a member of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) and a senior member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE). His spouse and co-petitioner, Margarita L. Fudim, held a degree in mechanical engineering from the Moscow Institute of Chemical Machine Building and, during 1986, 1987, and 1988, was employed as a computer programmer at Pansophic Systems, first in Oakbrook and then in Lisle, Illinois.

In 1985, Dr. Fudim formed Light Sculpting Co., which was his sole trade or business during the years at issue and whose income and deductions he reported on Schedule C, to research and develop an innovative manufacturing methodology known as "rapid modeling"—also referred to in engineering literature as "rapid prototyping" or "desktop manufacturing". The rapid modeling process utilized ultraviolet (UV) light and light-sensitive liquid polymers (photopolymers) to fabricate three-dimensional plastic objects directly from instructions generated by a computer-aided design (CAD) system. This technological breakthrough enabled complex three-dimensional industrial models to be fabricated in minutes rather than months. Because it is difficult for light to penetrate thick layers of polymer (thereby requiring multiple layers to be formed), Dr. Fudim also attempted to perfect the rapid modeling process by looking for alternatives, such as heat and ultrasonic energy, to solidify the parts when relatively thick models were to be formed. His research at Light Sculpting Co. yielded two United States patents—issued on June 21, 1988, and January 31, 1989—and led to his work being featured in numerous articles in both scientific and popular publications, while a number of major corporations, including ALCOA, DuPont, Ford, Chrysler, and United Technologies, became interested in his rapid modeling process.
The Taxpayer's Claim and Quantitative Breakdown

The petitioners claimed federal R&D tax credits under IRC Section 41 of $2,890 on their 1987 return and $6,176 on their 1988 return (to which a Form 6765 was attached); although the parties stipulated that a research credit was also claimed for 1986, the court was unable to find an entry for that credit on the 1986 return, but because of the stipulation it decided entitlement to a 1986 credit as well. The claimed QREs were derived from three distinct cost components incurred by Light Sculpting Co., encompassing physical supplies consumed in the experimental process, Dr. Fudim's net self-employment earnings reported on Schedule C, and wages paid to part-time family employees, specifically Mrs. Margarita Fudim and the petitioners' daughter, Natalia Fudim.

During the years at issue, in addition to his research activities, Dr. Fudim did some consulting work for Sundstrand, which paid him on average $1,500 per day, and he was also paid a small amount for writing and reviewing scientific articles. On his Schedule C filings for Light Sculpting Co., which reported his consulting fees ($17,220, $53,604, and $63,842), modeling process receipts, and scientific paper fees, Dr. Fudim reported gross receipts or income and business deductions that resulted in net self-employment income of $3,027 in 1986, $18,504 in 1987, and $48,035 in 1988. He asserted that he devoted 3,000 hours (90.76 percent of his total working hours) to R&D in 1986—spending only 305.5 hours on external consulting—and that he devoted at least 80 percent of his total time to qualified research in both 1987 and 1988.

To assist with technical tasks, Dr. Fudim employed Mrs. Fudim on a part-time basis, and she assisted him from May through December 1987 with designing, drafting, and performing experiments. She was compensated at $16.00 per hour for 600 hours of work, totaling $9,600, which Dr. Fudim reported on a Form W-2 and which she reported on the couple's 1987 joint federal income tax return. The petitioners claimed that 480 hours, or 80.00 percent of Mrs. Fudim's time, constituted qualified research services. Additionally, Dr. Fudim employed his daughter, Natalia Fudim—whom the petitioners claimed as a dependent across all three tax years—as a part-time worker paid between $6.40 and $8.00 per hour. Natalia was issued Forms W-2 reporting wages of $4,800 in 1986, $5,900 in 1987, and $9,859 in 1988, with the petitioners claiming that she devoted 83.33 percent, 69.81 percent, and 80.00 percent of her time to R&D in those respective years. Finally, the supplies deducted on Schedule C included research supplies of $430 in 1986, $2,295 in 1987, and $3,863 in 1988 for photopolymers, alcohol or other solvents used to wash out the polymer, photo masks to control UV light exposure, light sources (bulbs and starters), cooling fans, photometers to measure light intensity, and timers.

body.text: Administrative Dispute and the Commissioner's Challenge

The controversy originated on July 17, 1989, when the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Kansas City Service Center notified the petitioners that the $6,176 research credit claimed on their 1988 return exceeded the statutory limitation governing general business credits under IRC Section 38(c). Because the general business credit could not exceed the excess of the taxpayer's net income tax over the greater of the tentative minimum tax for the taxable year or 25 percent of so much of the taxpayer's net regular tax liability as exceeds $25,000, the IRS disallowed $3,222 of the 1988 credit and directed the petitioners either to explain why they had not erred or to remit $3,222. Following an examination of their books between November 1989 and January 1990, the examining agent's report allowed the reduced research credits after applying the IRC Section 38(c)(1) limitation and carrying the excess back to 1985; the petitioners signed that report on February 1, 1990, and the District Director accepted it on February 28, 1990, but a reviewer then concluded that the research credit had not been properly evaluated, the case was reassigned to a more experienced auditor and reopened by notice dated October 5, 1990, and the petitioners refused to cooperate or meet with the auditor. On March 1, 1991, the Commissioner issued a statutory Notice of Deficiency for 1986, 1987, and 1988 disallowing the research credits (along with the time share condominium losses and a portion of the charitable contributions), after which a March 4, 1991 notice threatened seizure of property within 30 days for the unpaid 1988 balance and a March 7, 1991 letter by Dr. Fudim's patent attorney to the IRS Problem Resolution Office failed to resolve the matter.

In litigation before the Tax Court, the Commissioner challenged both the foundational eligibility of Light Sculpting Co.'s activities as "qualified research" under IRC Section 41 and the substantiation of the claimed supply and wage QREs. Crucially, at trial Dr. Fudim produced summaries, but no contemporaneous records, of the time that he, Mrs. Fudim, and Natalia Fudim spent on research and development, claiming that he threw the contemporaneous records away after the Commissioner completed the initial audit of his books, so the court had to rely on his testimony and other evidence in the record to determine the time spent performing qualified services. In turn, the petitioners raised several threshold procedural defenses, asserting that their signing of the examining agent's report (which contained waiver language almost identical to Form 870) and the Commissioner's acceptance of it finally determined their tax liabilities, an argument the court treated as equating that acceptance with a closing agreement under IRC Section 7121; that the statute of limitations for 1986 had expired; that the burden of proof should shift to the Commissioner because the case was improperly reopened, which the court analyzed under the IRC Section 7605(b) restriction on a second inspection of books without written notice; and that the excess 1988 credit had been improperly assessed without a notice of deficiency.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The Tax Court evaluated the dispute under IRC Section 41 as in effect for the years at issue and its corresponding Treasury Regulations, under which the credit equaled 20 percent of the amount by which current qualified research expenses exceeded the average of such expenses over the preceding 3 years and, for taxable years after 1985, formed part of the general business credit under IRC Section 38. Under IRC Section 41(d)(1), as the court summarized it (citing TSR, Inc. v. Commissioner, 96 T.C. 903 (1991)), "qualified research" is research of a type whose expenditures are deductible under IRC Section 174, undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature and whose application is intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component of the taxpayer. To claim the credit, a taxpayer must incur QREs—consisting of "in-house research expenses" and "contract research expenses"—while carrying on a trade or business under IRC Section 41(b)(1). Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and (ii), in-house research expenses comprise wages paid or incurred to an employee for "qualified services" and amounts paid or incurred for "supplies" used in the conduct of qualified research. For sole proprietors and self-employed individuals, IRC Section 41(b)(2)(D)(ii), by cross-reference to IRC Sections 401(c)(1) and (2), expands the definition of "wages" to include earned income, defined as net earnings from self-employment reported on Schedule C.

Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B), "qualified services" are strictly limited to services consisting of engaging in qualified research, or engaging in the direct supervision or direct support of research activities that constitute qualified research. Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3)(ii) delineates the boundary of "direct support," specifying that qualifying support includes typing laboratory reports describing research results, cleaning laboratory equipment used in research, compiling research data, or machining a component of an experimental model, while excluding general administrative services and other services only indirectly of benefit to research activities.

Where an employee or self-employed researcher performs both qualified and nonqualified services during a taxable year, Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(d)(1) mandates that, absent a more appropriate method demonstrated by the taxpayer, reportable in-house wage QREs must be calculated by multiplying total wages by the ratio of total time spent performing qualified services to total time spent performing all services. However, IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(d)(2) establish the "substantially all" safe harbor rule: if at least 80 percent of the services performed by an employee for the taxpayer during a taxable year constitute qualified services, then 100 percent of that individual's wages are treated as in-house research expenses. Finally, any resulting research credit is integrated into the general business credit and subject to the tax liability ceiling imposed by IRC Section 38(c)(1).
The Tax Court's Holding

Special Trial Judge Pate delivered a split holding that handed the petitioners a substantial substantive victory on their core R&D activities while penalizing their evidentiary omissions regarding their daughter's employment and rejecting their procedural challenges. First, on the procedural issues, the court held that signing an examining agent's report or a Form 870, and its acceptance by the Commissioner, does not constitute a closing agreement under IRC Section 7121, which is the only statutorily authorized method of finalizing a tax liability (citing Botany Worsted Mills v. United States, 278 U.S. 282 (1929), and holding the report and Form 870 merely waive the notice requirements of IRC Section 6213(a)), that IRS Publication 1035 did not estop the Commissioner and the 1986 statute of limitations, extended by Form 872 to April 15, 1991, remained open, and that the Commissioner did not violate IRC Section 7605(b) because, the petitioners having refused to cooperate with the auditor, no second inspection of their books ever occurred (applying the rule of Ballantine v. Commissioner, 74 T.C. 516 (1980)). The court also held that claiming a credit in excess of the IRC Section 38(c)(1) limitation was a "mathematical or clerical error" under IRC Section 6213(g)(2)(E) that could be assessed without a notice of deficiency, that offsetting the petitioners' 1989 and 1990 refunds against the 1988 balance was proper, and, separately, that the petitioners' time share condominium losses were not deductible under IRC Section 280A.

Second, on the merits of IRC Section 41, the court stated it had "no doubt" that during 1986, 1987, and 1988 Dr. Fudim was engaged in research and development for which a credit is allowable, relying on his training and background, contemporaneous letters and scientific articles describing the process, and, most importantly, the two patents. Third, the court allowed 100 percent of the claimed research supply costs ($430 in 1986, $2,295 in 1987, and $3,863 in 1988) as valid QREs under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(ii). Fourth, addressing the absence of contemporaneous timecards, the court invoked Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), to estimate the qualified time allocations of the personnel. Relying on Dr. Fudim's testimony and other evidence in the record (for Dr. Fudim, his consulting days derived from his average $1,500 daily rate and the small amount of time he spent on articles; for Mrs. Fudim, her engineering training and programming expertise), the court determined that both Dr. Fudim (in 1986, 1987, and 1988) and Mrs. Fudim (in 1987) spent at least 80 percent of their working time performing qualified services, thereby qualifying 100 percent of Dr. Fudim's Schedule C net self-employment income and 100 percent of Mrs. Fudim's 1987 wages for the credit under the IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) "substantially all" rule. Conversely, the court found it did not have sufficient information to determine whether the services of Natalia Fudim were qualified services, disallowing 100 percent of her wages across all three years because the record did not reveal her age, training, or level of expertise and no evidence was presented as to what services she rendered. The court directed that the petitioners' research credits and allowable carrybacks for 1986, 1987, and 1988 be recomputed under Tax Court Rule 155.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures
Spoliation and Absence of Contemporaneous Time-Tracking Records

The central evidentiary crisis in Fudim stemmed from the absence of contemporaneous time records, which Dr. Fudim claimed he had thrown away. Under IRC Section 6001 and the burden of proof principles articulated in Tax Court Rule 142(a) and Welch v. Helvering, 290 U.S. 111, 115 (1933), tax credits are a matter of legislative grace, and the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of substantiating both the eligibility of the underlying activities and the precise quantification of the claimed QREs. According to Dr. Fudim, contemporaneous records of time existed, but he claimed he threw them away after the Commissioner completed the initial audit of his books; the opinion does not state his reason, although the petitioners separately argued that their acceptance of the examining agent's report had closed their case. Consequently, at trial, Dr. Fudim produced only summaries, without contemporaneous records, of the time spent by himself, his wife, and his daughter, and the court relied on his testimony and other evidence in the record.

This evidentiary deficiency exposed the petitioners to the risk of total disallowance under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(d)(1), which requires a verifiable nexus between wages paid and the ratio of hours devoted to qualified services versus total hours worked. While the Tax Court ultimately allowed Dr. Fudim's and Mrs. Fudim's wage claims through judicial estimation, the absence of contemporaneous records, combined with the lack of any evidence of Natalia's age, training, expertise, or services, resulted in the complete disallowance of the credit attributable to their daughter's compensation. Furthermore, as the court held in rejecting the petitioners' procedural arguments, signing an examining agent's report or Form 870, and its acceptance by the Commissioner, is not a closing agreement under IRC Section 7121 and merely waives the notice requirements of IRC Section 6213(a); the practical lesson, although not stated by the court, is that primary substantiation records should be retained until all statutory assessment and carryforward or carryback periods have expired.
The Evidentiary Dichotomy Under the Cohan Rule: Corroborated Technical Credibility Versus Unsubstantiated Familial Claims

A critical legal takeaway from Fudim lies in how Special Trial Judge Pate bifurcated the application of the Cohan doctrine across the three individuals whose compensation was claimed as QREs. Under Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), when a taxpayer establishes that they actually engaged in qualified activities and incurred deductible or creditable expenses, but cannot substantiate the exact dollar or hour figure due to inadequate recordkeeping, the court may approximate the allowable amount, "bearing heavily if it chooses upon the taxpayer whose inexactitude is of his own making". However, Cohan is not an automatic mandate to guess; to trigger judicial estimation, the taxpayer must first construct a credible evidentiary foundation providing the court with a rational basis upon which to make an informed estimate.

For Dr. Fudim, the record contained objective evidence and an arithmetic basis that supported his testimony and allowed the court to estimate his time allocation, while for Mrs. Fudim the court relied on her engineering training and programming expertise. First, the record contained objective evidence that qualified research was being performed, meaning the court did not have to rely solely on Dr. Fudim's testimony; the court pointed to his training and background, contemporaneous letters and scientific articles acknowledging and describing his newly developed rapid modeling process, and, most importantly, two U.S. patents (June 21, 1988, and January 31, 1989) reflecting the results of his research during 1986, 1987, and 1988, while the findings of fact also noted that major corporations (ALCOA, DuPont, Ford, Chrysler, and United Technologies) had become interested in the process.

Second, the court relied on a mathematical reconstruction of non-research consulting time to bound Dr. Fudim's R&D activities. Because Light Sculpting Co. was his sole trade or business, Dr. Fudim's Schedule C gross receipts combined consulting fees (paid by Sundstrand) and a small amount for scientific papers with modeling process receipts. The court estimated his consulting time on the basis that Sundstrand paid him, on average, $1,500 per day. At that rate, the court estimated that Dr. Fudim worked approximately 12 days in 1986, 36 days in 1987, and 43 days in 1988 for Sundstrand (by comparison, Dr. Fudim himself claimed 305.5 consulting hours for 1986). Noting also that he spent only a small amount of time writing and reviewing articles, the court found that, even assuming he worked only a 5-day week (and it was convinced he worked more), he spent more than 80 percent of his time performing qualified services, satisfying the threshold under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B).

Third, the court relied on Mrs. Fudim's technical qualifications to validate her allocation. For Mrs. Fudim, the petitioners claimed exactly 480 hours out of 600 hours worked (80.00 percent) from May through December 1987. During that period she was also employed as a computer programmer at Pansophic Systems, and her formal credentials consisted of a mechanical engineering degree from the Moscow Institute of Chemical Machine Building combined with computer programming expertise. The findings of fact state that she assisted Dr. Fudim with designing, drafting, and performing experiments, and the court concluded that she spent at least 80 percent of her 1987 time on qualified services because she is a highly trained engineer proficient in computer programming who, with that expertise, "had to have been a substantial help" to her husband, thereby triggering the "substantially all" rule to allow 100 percent of her $9,600 wages.
Total Evidentiary Failure Regarding Dependent Family Member Wages

In stark contrast to the allowance of Mrs. Fudim's compensation, the petitioners suffered a total disqualification regarding the $20,559 in cumulative wages paid to their daughter, Natalia Fudim ($4,800 in 1986, $5,900 in 1987, and $9,859 in 1988). While Dr. Fudim complied with formal payroll reporting by issuing Forms W-2 to Natalia and paying her an hourly wage between $6.40 and $8.00, payroll compliance merely proves that compensation was paid—it does not establish that the underlying labor constituted "qualified services" under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B).

Special Trial Judge Pate identified four evidentiary gaps regarding Natalia's employment: the record failed to reveal her age, her training, or her level of expertise, and the petitioners failed to present any evidence as to what services she rendered. First, the petitioners failed to establish her age; although they claimed a dependency exemption for Natalia on their joint tax returns for 1986, 1987, and 1988, the record did not reveal her age during the years at issue, leaving no basis for assessing her capacity to perform research-related services. Second, there was a complete absence of evidence of training or expertise; unlike Dr. and Mrs. Fudim, whose Soviet academic degrees and professional engineering backgrounds were established in the record, the record did not reveal Natalia's training or level of expertise.

Third, the petitioners failed to delineate specific "direct support" tasks. Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3)(ii), a non-scientist or lower-wage assistant can still generate eligible QREs if they perform "direct support" of research—such as cleaning photopolymer vats, washing cured models with alcohol solvents, compiling experimental light-intensity data, or typing laboratory reports. However, the petitioners failed to present any evidence as to what services Natalia rendered. Without task-level evidence, the court could not determine whether she was performing qualifying direct laboratory support under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3)(ii) or excluded general administrative, clerical, or bookkeeping tasks. Fourth, although the court did not rely on this point, the petitioners' retrospective summaries asserted precise allocation percentages, claiming that Natalia devoted exactly 83.33 percent in 1986, 69.81 percent in 1987, and 80.00 percent in 1988 to R&D, without any contemporaneous records to show how those percentages were derived. Concluding that it "simply" did not have sufficient information to determine whether Natalia's services were directed to qualified research, the court held that the petitioners were not entitled to any research credit based on the wages paid to her.
Procedural Missteps and General Business Credit Limitations Under IRC Section 38(c)

Beyond the substantiation of QREs, Fudim highlights a critical statutory limitation that frequently traps innovative pass-through entities and sole proprietors: the interplay between IRC Section 41 and the general business credit tax liability ceiling under IRC Section 38(c)(1). For the 1988 tax year, the petitioners claimed a research credit of $6,176 and, although the attached Form 6765 contained an explanation of the limitation, ignored it and reduced their tax by the full amount. However, IRC Section 38(c)(1) dictates that the allowable general business credit for any taxable year cannot exceed the excess of the taxpayer's "net income tax" over the greater of the tentative minimum tax for the taxable year, or 25 percent of so much of the taxpayer's net regular tax liability as exceeds $25,000.

Because the Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) regime created a tentative minimum tax floor, the petitioners' usable credit for 1988 was statutorily capped, resulting in the immediate administrative disallowance of $3,222 of the claimed $6,176 credit (although the IRS letter cited IRC Section 38(c)(1)(B), the court observed that the adjustment appears to have been computed under IRC Section 38(c)(1)(A)). The petitioners did recognize that the disallowed portion was not permanently lost but converted into an unused general business credit eligible for carryback (then 3 years, currently 1 year under IRC Section 39) and carryforward (then 15 years, currently 20 years): they asked that the excess be carried back to 1985, 1986, and 1987, filed amended returns carrying back the $3,222 and claiming refunds of $2,643 for 1985 and $579 for 1986, and the examining agent's report allowed the carryback to 1985. Nevertheless, the petitioners also disputed the Kansas City Service Center's demands for payment, objected to the offset of their 1989 refund, refused to cooperate or meet with the auditor after their case was reopened, and unsuccessfully argued that their acceptance of the examining agent's report barred further adjustments.
Second-Order Jurisprudential Implications: The Narrowing of Fudim in Modern Section 41 Litigation

From a strategic litigation perspective, Fudim v. Commissioner represents the high-water mark of judicial leniency under the Cohan rule in R&D tax credit disputes. In subsequent decades, taxpayers repeatedly cited Fudim (alongside the Fifth Circuit's decision in United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009)) for the proposition that the Tax Court is legally required to estimate wage QREs whenever a company proves that some qualified research occurred. However, modern United States federal tax jurisprudence has sharply circumscribed Fudim, establishing a strict two-step gatekeeping standard that renders reliance on oral estimates fatal in the vast majority of contemporary examinations.

Specifically, in Shami v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2012-78, aff'd in part, 741 F.3d 560 (5th Cir. 2014), the taxpayers relied on McFerrin and Cohan to support estimated R&D time allocations for two executives, Farouk Shami and John McCall, whose wages accounted for over 80 percent of the claimed wage QREs, without documentation of the time they spent on qualified services. The Tax Court declined to make an estimate, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed that refusal, holding that Cohan does not compel an estimate unless the taxpayer proves some qualified services were performed and the record provides a reasonable basis for one, and deferring to the Tax Court's rejection of testimony it found general, vague, conclusory, self-serving, and unreliable, resulting in a zero percent allowance for those wages (although the Fifth Circuit vacated in part on a separate issue concerning supply QREs the Commissioner had conceded). Similarly, in Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, the Tax Court allowed estimated wage QREs for the CEO of a business telephone systems company only on the basis of extensive witness testimony and documentary evidence in the record, while finding part of his compensation unreasonable under the IRC Section 174(e) reasonableness standard. Furthermore, regarding supply QREs, whereas the court found Dr. Fudim's $6,588 in cumulative research supplies were devoted to his research, with no evidence of their use in his consulting work, subsequent appellate precedent in Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), established that raw materials and supplies used during commercial production runs do not qualify under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) if those supplies would have been purchased regardless of the process experimentation. Thus, Fudim succeeds as a shield only when the taxpayer's oral testimony is anchored by indisputable scientific credentials, patented inventions, segregated experimental materials, and verifiable arithmetic boundaries on non-research activities.

Contemporaneous Record Retention & Audit Finality
IRC § 6001; IRC § 7121; IRC § 7605(b); Tax Ct. Rule 142(a)
Dr. Fudim claimed he threw away contemporaneous time records after the initial audit; separately, petitioners argued that signing the examining agent's report closed their case.

Signing an examining agent's report or Form 870 is not a closing agreement under § 7121; as a practical matter (not a holding of the court), taxpayers should retain primary records across all open assessment and credit carryback/forward years.

Failed Procedurally: Court rejected the § 7121, statute of limitations, and § 7605(b) arguments; separately, the absence of contemporaneous records required Cohan estimates and contributed to the disallowance of Natalia's wages.
General Business Credit Tax Liability Ceiling
Petitioners claimed $6,176 credit in 1988 without applying the tentative minimum tax / net regular tax liability limitation.

Allowable credit is strictly capped by the excess of net income tax over the greater of tentative minimum tax or 25% of so much of net regular tax liability as exceeds $25,000; excess carries back/forward.

Upheld Statutory Cap: Claiming credit above the § 38(c)(1) limit was a mathematical or clerical error under § 6213(g)(2)(E), assessable without a notice of deficiency, and refund offsets were proper; research credits and allowable carrybacks are recomputed under Rule 155.

body.text: Applied Remedial Case Studies
Case Study 1: Advanced Additive Manufacturing Startup (Owner-Operator Self-Employment Income, Familial Direct Support, and Prototype Supply Tracking)
Scenario and Identified Legal Pitfalls

Photonic Layer Systems LLC ("PLS"), a single-member limited liability company treated as a disregarded entity taxed as a sole proprietorship on Schedule C and based in Austin, Texas, is founded by Dr. Elena Vance, a Ph.D. materials scientist. PLS is developing a multi-wavelength laser sintering and photopolymerization apparatus capable of printing biocompatible ceramic-polymer composite implants. To finance PLS without institutional venture capital, Dr. Vance performs high-rate forensic failure analysis consulting for aerospace contractors, billing $2,000 per day under the same Schedule C entity, yet she fails to keep daily timecards separating her consulting hours from her laser sintering R&D. Furthermore, Dr. Vance employs her husband, a full-time software architect at an enterprise technology firm, on a part-time basis for 500 hours during the year to write custom G-code slicing algorithms, paying him $15,000 on Form W-2. She also employs her 19-year-old undergraduate sophomore son part-time for 800 hours at $15.00 per hour ($12,000 on Form W-2), claiming him as a dependent on her joint Form 1040. On Form 6765, Dr. Vance claims 85 percent of her net Schedule C income, 80 percent of her husband's wages, and 75 percent of her son's wages as QREs based purely on year-end retrospective estimates, while discarding her laboratory wall calendars after filing. In an IRS examination under the standards of Fudim and Shami, while Dr. Vance's patents and her husband's software credentials might survive scrutiny, the IRS examining agent will disallow 100 percent of her son's $12,000 wages due to the lack of evidence proving his technical qualifications or specific "direct support" tasks under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3)(ii), and may challenge Dr. Vance's Schedule C net income allocation due to commingled consulting expenses and missing contemporaneous time logs.
Step-by-Step Remediation Blueprint

First, to satisfy IRC Section 41(d)(2)(A) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(b)(2) regarding project governance and business component architecture, PLS must formally segregate its activities at the inception of the tax year into discrete business components. Dr. Vance must establish a digital Project Charter System that separates Non-Qualifying Commercial Consulting (Cost Center 100) from specific R&D business components, specifically BC-201 (Dual-Wavelength Optical Delivery Head) and BC-202 (Ceramic-Photopolymer Resin Formulation). For each business component, the project charter must contemporaneously document the four statutory elements of IRC Section 41(d)(1), identifying the specific technological uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design (such as achieving uniform curing depth above 5 millimeters without thermal micro-cracking), the scientific principles of materials science, optics, and thermodynamics relied upon, and the structured process of experimentation encompassing hypothesis formulation, computer modeling, iterative physical test builds, and photometer or tensile validation.

Second, to eliminate reliance on the precarious Cohan estimation rule and prevent the record-destruction pitfall of Fudim, PLS must deploy a cloud-based, immutable time-tracking system coupled with a mandatory ten-year tax record retention policy that preserves all primary logs across open statutory assessment and credit carryforward periods. Every individual working at PLS—Dr. Vance, her spouse, and her son—must log hours weekly against three-tier activity codes: QUAL-PERF for direct performance of qualified research under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B)(i); QUAL-SUPP for direct supervision or direct support of research under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3)(ii); and NON-QUAL for external aerospace consulting, patent prosecution administration, general bookkeeping, and marketing. By tracking hours contemporaneously, if Dr. Vance logs 2,200 hours on QUAL-PERF and 300 hours on NON-QUAL consulting (88.0 percent qualified), she mathematically locks in the 80 percent "substantially all" safe harbor under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(d)(2), entitling PLS to claim 100 percent of its eligible net Schedule C self-employment earnings without judicial haircutting.

Third, to overcome the specific evidentiary failures that doomed Natalia Fudim's wages in Fudim and that forced the court to estimate Dr. Fudim's time from his consulting income, PLS must execute rigorous contractual and employment structuring for both consulting operations and family personnel. Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(D)(ii) and Section 401(c)(1), self-employment "earned income" is net of allowable trade or business deductions, requiring Dr. Vance to maintain separate general ledger sub-accounts for her aerospace consulting engagement letters (tracking exact days billed at $2,000 per day alongside dedicated travel expenses) versus PLS laboratory expenses so that the IRS can verify both her time ratio and her net earned income base. To substantiate the dependent son's $12,000 W-2 wages under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3)(ii), PLS must compile a contemporaneous Personnel Qualification and Direct Support Dossier containing a formal written job description titled Laboratory Research Support Technician that explicitly prohibits general office or administrative errands during logged R&D hours, documentary proof of his age, university enrollment in chemistry or mechanical engineering coursework, and laboratory safety training certifications. This dossier must be paired with daily work logs signed by Dr. Vance detailing specific qualifying direct support activities explicitly enumerated in Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3)(ii), such as cleaning uncured ceramic-photopolymer vats with isopropyl alcohol solvent following experimental builds, machining aluminum mounting brackets for the UV photometer sensor array, and compiling laser power-density and cure-depth measurements into the laboratory database. For Dr. Vance's husband, PLS must retain his academic degrees and resume, a written part-time employment agreement specifying his $30.00 per hour market-supported wage rate, and Git version-control commit logs showing timestamps and code check-ins for the G-code slicing algorithms tied directly to BC-201.

Fourth, to mirror the successful substantiation of supplies in Fudim while insulating against Union Carbide challenges, PLS must establish a dedicated general ledger account (GL 5120 - R&D Experimental Supplies). Every purchase order and vendor invoice for ceramic powders, liquid photopolymers, chemical wash solvents, laser diodes, optical mirrors, cooling fans, and photometers must be stamped with the corresponding Business Component ID (BC-201 or BC-202) and linked in the laboratory notebook to the specific experimental build in which the materials were consumed. Any depreciable capital equipment, such as oscilloscopes or CNC mills, must be segregated into fixed asset accounts (GL 1500) so that only non-depreciable tangible supplies consumed in research are claimed under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(ii).
Case Study 2: Industrial Chemical and Polymer Processing Enterprise (Multi-Departmental Wage Allocation, Executive Technical Supervision, and General Business Credit Optimization)
Scenario and Identified Legal Pitfalls

Midwest Specialty Polymers Inc. ("MSP"), an S corporation headquartered in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, manufactures industrial adhesives and UV-curable coatings and undertakes a major initiative during the tax year to develop a solvent-free, ultrasonic-cured polymer coating process for automotive body panels. MSP claims $1.2 million in wage QREs, 60 percent of which derives from the W-2 salaries of its Chief Executive Officer—a former chemical engineer who claims 80 percent of his time under the "substantially all" rule—and four Plant Process Engineers who split their time between routine commercial quality control and experimental ultrasonic curing trials. No timesheets exist; instead, MSP relies on an oral interview survey conducted 14 months after year-end, citing Fudim as authority for estimating the 80 percent threshold. Additionally, MSP claims $450,000 in raw polymer feedstocks used during plant-scale trial runs where the resulting coated panels were subsequently sold to commercial customers. Compounding these substantive risks, MSP's shareholders are subject to high tentative minimum tax liabilities on their individual returns and fail to model the IRC Section 38(c)(1) general business credit limitation or make a timely IRC Section 280C(c)(2) reduced credit election on MSP's original S corporation return, triggering IRS Service Center deficiency notices and underpayment penalties.
Step-by-Step Remediation Blueprint

First, to prevent the total disallowance of process research expenses seen in Little Sandy Coal and Union Carbide, MSP must institute a formal Phase-Gate R&D Governance Protocol that strictly separates process R&D from commercial production under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(C) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii). Because IRC Section 41(d)(2)(C) treats a plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production as a separate business component from the product being produced, MSP must charter Project UP-400 (Ultrasonic Polymer Curing Process) independently of the commercial automotive panels. Prior to any plant trial, the engineering team must generate a formal Experimental Trial Protocol documenting the specific technological uncertainty (such as ultrasonic transducer cavitation causing uneven cross-linking in polymer layers thicker than 2 millimeters), the specific variables being systematically altered (ultrasonic frequency, amplitude, feed speed, and catalyst ratios), and the baseline mathematical models being tested.

Second, to survive the heightened scrutiny of Shami and satisfy the corroboration standard of Fudim and Suder for non-timecard personnel, MSP must replace post-hoc oral surveys with contemporaneous corroborative anchoring. For the four hybrid Plant Process Engineers, MSP must implement bi-weekly digital project allocation certifications tied directly to plant scheduling software; whenever the production line is taken offline for an experimental ultrasonic curing trial (UP-400), the plant Manufacturing Execution System (MES) must automatically log the exact start and stop timestamps alongside the badge-swiped engineers present on the floor. Regarding the CEO, Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(2) restricts "direct supervision" to immediate first-line management of qualified research, excluding higher-level executives unless they personally conduct or directly supervise the technical experiments. To substantiate the CEO's time, MSP must compile an Executive Technical Portfolio containing Outlook calendar logs, engineering design review minutes, redlined chemical and mechanical schematics personally authored by the CEO, alpha-testing sign-off sheets proving hands-on technical evaluation of every prototype run (as validated in Suder), patent applications listing the CEO as a named inventor on the ultrasonic curing technology (as validated in Fudim), and a compensation benchmarking study separating the CEO's base technical salary from corporate performance bonuses to ensure compliance with the IRC Section 174(e) reasonableness mandate. Rather than aggressively claiming an unsupported 80 percent "substantially all" figure for the CEO—which invites total disallowance under Shami—MSP must calculate the exact ratio of corroborated technical hours to total hours worked under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(d)(1), claiming a rigorously documented fractional allocation.

Third, where MSP engages external testing laboratories or university metallurgy departments to evaluate cured polymer samples, it must structure its vendor agreements to comply with the contract research rules of IRC Section 41(b)(3) and avoid the funded research exclusion under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H). All third-party testing contracts must explicitly stipulate that the research services are performed on behalf of MSP prior to commercial production, that MSP retains exclusive and substantial rights to all research results and intellectual property without paying additional royalties, and that MSP bears the full financial risk of the research by paying on a time-and-materials or milestone basis contingent on successful technical performance rather than guaranteed commercial output.

Fourth, to eliminate the supply disqualification trap of Union Carbide and the credit utilization dispute of Fudim, MSP must implement strict supply ledger segregation and pre-filing tax liability modeling prior to filing Form 6765. Because Union Carbide prohibits claiming raw materials used to manufacture goods that are ultimately sold to customers as supply QREs under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), MSP must restrict its supply QRE claims strictly to dedicated lab-scale and pilot-line batches (GL 5150 - Dedicated Pilot Trial Supplies) where the resulting polymer-coated panels are subjected to destructive tensile and weathering testing and subsequently scrapped, while excluding raw feedstocks used in commercial production batches. Simultaneously, before filing its timely S corporation tax return, MSP's tax advisors must execute a timely IRC Section 280C(c)(2) reduced credit election on the original return—preventing the mandatory add-back of the gross credit amount to taxable income that otherwise inflates net income tax and exacerbates AMT exposure—and calculate each shareholder's exact IRC Section 38(c)(1) general business credit limitation by comparing net income tax against tentative minimum tax and the 25 percent net regular tax liability threshold. By reporting only the statutorily usable portion on the current year return and establishing a formal General Business Credit Carryback and Carryforward Ledger (1-year carryback and 20-year carryforward under IRC Section 39), the taxpayers preserve all excess credits across future tax years without triggering IRS Service Center disallowance notices.

body.text: Conclusion and Strategic Practice Directives

The United States Tax Court's decision in Fudim v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1994-235, stands as a dual-edged precedent in federal R&D tax credit practice. On one hand, the ruling confirms that genuine technological innovators—particularly closely held businesses and sole proprietors developing patented, industry-disrupting technologies—can include owner self-employment income, qualified family member wages, and experimental prototyping supplies in their IRC Section 41 credit base, and may survive the absence of formal timesheets if the record is fortified by objective scientific credentials, external technical validation, and verifiable mathematical boundaries on non-research activities. On the other hand, the court's summary rejection of the wages paid to the petitioner's daughter, alongside the subsequent judicial tightening in Shami and Suder, demonstrates that the Cohan estimation doctrine cannot cure an evidentiary vacuum. To insulate R&D tax credit claims against IRS examination, taxpayers and technical tax advisors must enforce contemporaneous project-level time tracking, maintain strict general ledger segregation between commercial operations and experimental trials, document the specific qualifications and direct-support tasks of all auxiliary personnel under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3)(ii), and retain all primary substantiation records across the entire statutory life of the credit and its carryforwards.
